definition.text: Small, grid-connected devices that generate and store electricity close to the load they serve, called distributed energy resources.

facts.text: Conventional power stations are centralised and often send power over long distances, whereas distributed energy resources are modular, sited near the load and have capacities of 10 MW or less.
Central plants' economies of scale began to fail in the late 1960s, and by the early 21st century they arguably could no longer deliver cheap, reliable power to remote customers through the grid.

Distributed energy resources include cogeneration, solar photovoltaics, small wind, microhydro, waste-to-energy and storage such as batteries, flywheels and vehicle-to-grid; they typically have high capital cost per kilowatt.
Integrating distributed sources raises technical problems of power quality, voltage stability, harmonics, reliability, protection and control; IEEE 1547 sets the interconnection standard.
Local production avoids transmission losses, which are generally 8-15% of energy on long lines and transformers.
Solar-plus-battery stand-alone systems have a low levelized cost, so some authors think they may enable mass grid defection.
A single vendor's vulnerable control system used at thousands of sites could let one attacker disable them all, reversing decentralisation's benefits.

definition.text: A localized grouping of generation, storage and loads that normally runs connected to the main grid but can disconnect and operate autonomously.

facts.text: A microgrid links to the macrogrid at a single point of common coupling, which can be disconnected.
Generation and loads in a microgrid are usually interconnected at low voltage and can run on DC, AC or both.

definition.text: The process of producing electric power from primary energy sources, carried out in power stations before delivery or storage.

facts.text: Electricity is not freely available in nature and must be produced by transforming other forms of energy; most is made by electromechanical generators driven by heat engines, flowing water or wind.
Only photovoltaic solar and fuel cells produce commercial-scale electricity without a generator; almost all other commercial power comes from a turbine.
World generation in 2024 was 30,850 TWh: coal 34%, gas 22%, hydro 14%, nuclear 9%, wind 8%, solar 7%, oil and other fossil 3%, biomass 2%.
Cleanliness depends on the source: fossil fuels supply about 10% of electricity in France, 70% in the US and 80% in China.
Coal plants supply about a third of world electricity but cause the most early deaths per unit of energy, mainly from air pollution.
Gas plants are more efficient than coal and emit less carbon dioxide, but gas extraction releases significant methane.
Hydropower supplied 15% of world electricity in 2023 and, with a dam and reservoir, can change output within seconds or minutes.
Grids carry varying loads; the daily minimum is the base load, often supplied by plants that run continuously.
